newsitem.title: FRANCE: Exporters fret over delivery cost of Saudi barley.
newsitem.headline: Exporters fret over delivery cost of Saudi barley.

text.p: Exporters awaiting the results of a huge barley import tender launched by Saudi Arabia are already fretting over the costs of late deliveries to congested Saudi ports.

Saudi Arabia appeared to be moving towards a final purchase of some 1.4 million tonnes of optional feed barley after tendering for 1.72 milion tonnes for delivery between October and December, grain traders said earlier.
Details of the purchase have yet to be confirmed and may become known later on Monday.

Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest importer of feed barley, may have decided to reduce the quantity it was buying in part because of firm prices but mostly because its ports have a limited capacity for handling the grain, traders said.
Saudi ports are still handling barley bought under a previous tender for 800,000 tonnes for September-October delivery.
The Saudis tapped world markets again for barley last week as prices had eased on prospects of bumper crops this year.
But prices have firmed again from as low as $130 per tonne, FOB last week on news of the new tender.
Given that Saudi ports can handle only 14,000 tonnes of barley per day, it would take roughly 100 days to deliver the grain, exporters said.

But the Saudi tender calls for deliveries over 56 days, they said. In fact because no exporter is in a position to deliver the grain during the first week of October, this limits deliveries to 48 days.
"Some 1.4 million tonnes is enormous. Exporters would need to deliver 29,200 tonnes per day to ship 1.4 million tonnes over 48 days," one trader said, adding this was not feasible.
He said this meant there may be delays in deliveries, with ships unloading until mid-February.
One trader estimated exporters will have to pay penalties of around $9 per day for delays in deliveries.
Traders said offers to the Saudi tender were between $146 and $164 a tonne, with freight.
One trader estimated that would make an average selling price of $158, with freight, if operators include the cost of paying for delayed deliveries.

Traders estimate up to one million tonnes may come from the European Union, which enjoys a supply and freight advantage over other suppliers, over 125,000 tonnes from Turkey and the rest coming from Canada and Australia.
Operators said a European Union export subsidy of over 30 Ecus per tonne would be needed to help cover a sale made at an average price of $158 per tonne, including freight.
